subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how data was shared so freely [Thinking]
passage:
Rajni, you asked what changed my habits, and it wasn't the breach itself. It was the question I asked afterwards: why did six different services already hold my name, my number and my birthday? Nobody forced me. I just typed it all in, every time, because the form had boxes.

So I traced it back. Most of those boxes were optional. I never read the permission screens either, I just pressed accept. That was the real root of it.

Now I give the minimum, and I skip optional fields. I made a separate email address only for sign-ups. And I read what an app asks for before saying yes, even if it takes a minute. I'm Tarun, and I've deleted four accounts I didn't need.

qa.q: What did Tarun make for sign-ups?
qa.a: A separate email address only for sign-ups.

qa.q: What might Tarun have been feeling when tracing the six services back to habit?
qa.a: Tarun was probably uneasy and a little embarrassed at having shared so freely, since habit and not any need was the real cause.

qa.q: What could Tarun do next to keep the new habit from slipping, and why?
qa.a: Tarun could check once a season which accounts still hold personal details and remove the ones not used, because habits need a regular reminder.

qa.q: How might Rajni, who asked the question, see Tarun's answer?
qa.a: Rajni may notice that Tarun blames the habit instead of the breach, which makes the answer useful to anyone who hears it.

grounding: Asking why so many services held the same details, the person decides to give minimum data, use a separate sign-up email and read permissions.
